name: FEVER
summary: 19,998 claims written by rewriting Wikipedia sentences, each labelled supported, refuted, or not verifiable from Wikipedia, with the sentences an annotator used to decide.
overview:
FEVER asks whether Wikipedia supports a claim. Each claim is a single short statement, averaging 9.4 words, and a system has to label it SUPPORTS, REFUTES, or NOT ENOUGH INFO and point at the Wikipedia sentences that justify the label. That second requirement is what sets FEVER apart from text classification: a label with the wrong evidence earns nothing, so the benchmark measures retrieval and judgement together. The dataset holds 185,445 claims and was published at NAACL-HLT 2018 by researchers at the University of Sheffield and Amazon. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05355)

The claims were manufactured rather than collected. Annotators were shown one sentence from the introduction of a popular English Wikipedia page, together with the first sentence of each page it linked to, and wrote a claim about the page's subject; they then produced altered versions of their own claim in six ways, by paraphrasing it, negating it, substituting a similar or a dissimilar entity, or making it more general or more specific. A second group of annotators, who saw the article but not the sentence the claim came from, assigned the label and marked the sentences they had used, adding other Wikipedia pages as evidence when they needed them. A claim was labelled NOT ENOUGH INFO when nothing in Wikipedia could settle it, which the mutations often produced by making a claim too specific or too vague. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05355)

The authors' own pipeline, which retrieved documents with DrQA, selected sentences by tf-idf, and classified with a decomposable attention model, labelled 50.91% of test claims correctly but scored 31.87% once the evidence had to be right too. The 2018 shared task closed much of that gap: the winning system, UNC-NLP, reached 68.21% label accuracy and a FEVER score of 64.21% with an evidence F1 of 0.53. FEVER has since become the standard benchmark for retrieval-grounded fact verification and the basis of several successor datasets, including an adversarial round in 2019 and the table-and-text FEVEROUS in 2021. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05355) and [shared task results](https://fever.ai/2018/task.html)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete labelled development split of the 2018 shared task, the published file `shared_task_dev.jsonl`: 19,998 claims, balanced at 6,666 SUPPORTS, 6,666 REFUTES, and 6,666 NOT ENOUGH INFO. The training split of 145,449 claims and the blind test split of 19,998, which is published without labels and scored by submission, are not imported. The two files the dataset page offers for reproducing the paper, `paper_dev.jsonl` and `paper_test.jsonl` with 9,999 claims each, were checked against this file: together they are exactly these 19,998 records, so the paper's development and test sets are both inside this snapshot. The file carries no version history, so it is pinned by its SHA-256 digest. [Development split](https://fever.ai/download/fever/shared_task_dev.jsonl)

Each Task Prompt is the claim, reproduced verbatim with nothing added. The claim is all a system is given: the dataset's own task is to find the evidence in Wikipedia, so no passage accompanies it, and the Solution carries the reference.

The Solution is the label, then every evidence set an annotator recorded, each listed as the page title, the sentence number as upstream records it counting from zero, and the sentence itself. Any one set is enough to justify the label, which is why several appear: 10,870 claims have one, 1,293 have two, 474 have three, 248 have four, 115 have five, and 332 have more, up to 32. The 6,666 claims labelled NOT ENOUGH INFO carry the label alone, as upstream records no evidence for them. Across the split the evidence cites 7,100 distinct sentences on 2,892 Wikipedia pages. The sentence text is not in the claims file: it comes from the authors' pre-processed Wikipedia archive, the June 2017 dump segmented with Stanford CoreNLP, which the importer reads and which is pinned by its own digest. Only the cited sentences are kept. Sentences and page titles keep that processing's spelling, so a space precedes punctuation and brackets are written `-LRB-` and `-RRB-`.

The importer uses only Python's standard library. It refuses either file if its digest differs, checks that each claim's evidence matches its label, and checks that every cited sentence exists and is not blank; 32 page titles are written in a different Unicode normalisation in the two files, so pages are matched by their normalised titles. The generated ATTRIBUTION.md credits all 2,892 cited articles with links, with the bracket and space escapes undone. Reading the 1.7 GB archive is the slow step; the import can be rerun with python3 data/fever/import.py.
scoring:
The shared task scores a system on its label and its evidence together. A system returns a label and a list of sentence addresses, of which only the first five count; evidence beyond that is discarded without penalty. The claim counts as correct only if the label is right and the returned sentences include at least one complete annotated evidence set. That measure is the FEVER score. Label accuracy, and precision, recall, and F1 over the evidence sentences, are reported as diagnostics and are used only to separate systems with equal FEVER scores. Claims labelled NOT ENOUGH INFO need no evidence, so for them the FEVER score is the label decision alone. [Scoring rules](https://fever.ai/2018/task.html)

Because one complete set suffices, a system is not penalised for choosing a different justification than the annotator did, as long as it returns all the sentences of some recorded set; multi-sentence claims therefore require every sentence of a set, not just the most informative one. Official numbers come from submitting to the blind test split, and numbers computed on this development split are self-reported. [Scoring program](https://github.com/sheffieldnlp/fever-scorer)

Benchopedia stores the claims, the labels, the evidence addresses, and the cited sentences. It does not run the scorer or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The claims are synthetic. They were written by annotators paraphrasing and mutating sentences from Wikipedia introductions, so they read like edited encyclopedia prose rather than the claims a fact-checker actually meets, and a refuted claim is usually a true sentence with one element changed. The NOT ENOUGH INFO class arose mostly from the same mutation process, which makes it a class of claims that are too specific or too general for Wikipedia rather than a sample of genuinely open questions. The authors found that annotators struggled with non-trivial negations and had to design the interface to discourage simply inserting "not". [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05355)

The evidence annotation is known to be incomplete. Measured against super-annotators, the recorded evidence had 95.42% precision but 72.36% recall, so a system that finds a correct and sufficient sentence the annotator did not mark is scored as wrong; the FEVER score's requirement that a returned set match a recorded one exactly is strict in the same direction. Agreement on the labels themselves was moderate, with a Fleiss kappa of 0.6841 over the 4% of claims annotated five ways, and the authors' own manual review found 91.2% of a 227-claim sample correctly annotated. A further 6.63% of collected claims were discarded as too vague or ambiguous. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.05355)

The world the claims are checked against is a fixed 2017 snapshot of about 50,000 popular Wikipedia pages, 5,000 of them the most-accessed pages and the rest linked from those, so it is skewed towards well-covered subjects and says nothing about claims whose answer is not in an article introduction. Only the introductions were offered as evidence. The text is tokenised in the style of the period and no article revision is recorded, so a reader checking Wikipedia today may not find the sentence that settled a claim. This development split is also balanced three ways by construction, unlike the training split, where supported claims outnumber refuted ones nearly three to one, so accuracy on it is not a figure a real stream of claims would produce.

The split has been public since 2018 and is widely used as training data for retrieval and entailment models, and it carries no canary string, so a model may have seen these claims, labels, and evidence in training; only the blind test split offers a measurement free of that doubt.
